questions.question: Which of the following is part of the Basis and Purpose of the Amateur Radio Service?
answers: Providing personal radio communications for as many citizens as possible
Advancing skills in the technical and communication phases of the radio art
questions.explanation: FCC Part 97.1 lists five purposes of the Amateur Radio Service; advancing skills in the technical and communication phases of the radio art is one of them. The others include emergency communications, international goodwill, and radio experimentation.

questions.question: Which agency regulates and enforces the rules for the Amateur Radio Service in the United States?
questions.explanation: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is the U.S. government agency that regulates amateur radio under Title 47 of the Code of Federal Regulations, Part 97.

questions.question: What do the FCC rules state regarding the use of a phonetic alphabet for station identification in the Amateur Radio Service?
answers: It is required when transmitting emergency messages
It is encouraged when using phone emissions
It is required when in contact with foreign stations
questions.explanation: FCC rules encourage (but do not require) the use of a standard phonetic alphabet when using phone emissions. Using phonetics helps ensure call signs are understood clearly, especially in poor conditions.

questions.question: How do you receive official notification of your new license and call sign after passing the exam?
answers: Email from the FCC with a link to download the license grant
USPS First-Class Mail from the FCC
Email from the lead volunteer examiner
USPS First-Class Mail from the lead volunteer examiner
questions.explanation: The FCC sends an email with a link to download the official license grant after it is issued. The FCC no longer mails paper licenses.

questions.question: What proves that the FCC has issued an operator/primary license grant?
answers: A printed copy of the certificate of successful completion of examination
An email notification from the NCVEC granting the license
The license appears in the FCC ULS database
questions.explanation: A license is officially granted when it appears in the FCC Universal Licensing System (ULS) database. A CSCE proves you passed the exam but is not the license itself.

questions.question: On which of the following HF frequencies can automatically controlled amateur propagation beacons be found?
answers: Anywhere in the Technician portion of 10 meters
Anywhere, if they are registered with the FCC
In a specific portion of each of the HF Technician bands
On ten meters, between 28.200 MHz and 28.300 MHz
questions.explanation: Per 97.203(d), automatically controlled propagation beacons on HF are restricted to 28.200–28.300 MHz on the 10-meter band.

questions.question: What is the FCC Part 97 definition of a space station?
answers: An amateur station located more than 50 km above Earth's surface
An amateur station using amateur radio satellites for relay of signals
questions.explanation: Part 97 defines a space station as an amateur station located more than 50 km above Earth's surface. This threshold distinguishes amateur space operations from terrestrial stations.

questions.question: Who recommends transmit/receive channels for repeater and auxiliary stations?
answers: A Frequency Spectrum Manager appointed by the FCC
A Volunteer Frequency Coordinator recognized by local amateurs
questions.explanation: Volunteer frequency coordinators, recognized by local amateur operators, recommend frequencies and operating parameters for repeater and auxiliary stations to minimize interference.

questions.question: Who selects a Frequency Coordinator?
answers: The FCC Office of Spectrum Management and Coordination Policy
The local chapter of the Office of National Council of Independent Frequency Coordinators
Amateur operators in a local or regional area whose stations are eligible to be repeater or auxiliary stations
questions.explanation: Frequency coordinators are selected by the amateur operators in a local or regional area whose stations are eligible to be repeater or auxiliary stations. This is a community-driven, volunteer process.

questions.question: Besides an FCC-issued amateur operator license, what is required to be the control operator of a Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service (RACES) Station?
answers: A written recommendation by the local ARRL Emergency Coordinator
Membership in the Amateur Radio Emergency Service (ARES)
Certification of current enrollment by a civil defense organization
questions.explanation: To operate a RACES station you must hold both a valid amateur license and current certification of enrollment in a civil defense organization. RACES is specifically for civil defense purposes.

questions.question: Which of the following is prohibited?
answers: International communications on VHF bands and higher frequencies
questions.explanation: FCC rules strictly prohibit willful or malicious interference to other amateur stations at all times. International communications and third-party digital traffic are generally permitted.

questions.question: Which of the following frequency ranges are available for phone operation by Technician licensees?
questions.explanation: Technician licensees have phone (voice) privileges on the 10-meter band from 28.300 to 28.500 MHz. Below 28.300 MHz, Technicians are limited to CW and data modes.

questions.question: Which of the following U.S. amateur radio operators are allowed to contact the International Space Station (ISS) on VHF bands?
answers: Only amateurs with a General class or higher license
Any amateur with a Technician class or higher license
Only amateurs with a General class or higher license, and NASA approval
Any amateurs with a Technician class or higher license, and NASA approval
questions.explanation: The ISS operates on VHF frequencies within the privileges of Technician class licensees, so any Technician or higher may contact the ISS. No special NASA approval is required.

questions.question: Which frequency is in the 6-meter amateur band?
questions.explanation: The 6-meter band spans 50–54 MHz, so 52.525 MHz falls within it. 49 MHz is below the band, 28.50 MHz is in the 10-meter band, and 222.15 MHz is in the 1.25-meter band.

questions.question: Which amateur band includes 146.52 MHz?
questions.explanation: The 2-meter band covers 144–148 MHz, which includes 146.52 MHz — the national FM simplex calling frequency. The 6-meter band covers 50–54 MHz and the 70 cm band covers 420–450 MHz.

questions.question: Which of the following bands include frequencies where Technicians are authorized to use digital modes such as FT8?
questions.explanation: Technician class operators are authorized to use digital modes in portions of the 10-meter, 6-meter, and 2-meter bands, so all these choices are correct.

questions.question: On which HF bands does a Technician class operator have phone privileges?
questions.explanation: Technician licensees have HF phone privileges only on a portion of the 10-meter band (28.300–28.500 MHz). On 80, 40, and 15 meters, Technicians are limited to CW only in small sub-bands.

questions.question: Which of the following VHF/UHF band segments are limited to CW only?
answers: 50.0 MHz to 50.1 MHz and 144.0 MHz to 144.1 MHz
219 MHz to 220 MHz and 420.0 MHz to 420.1 MHz
questions.explanation: The bottom 100 kHz of both the 6-meter band (50.0–50.1 MHz) and the 2-meter band (144.0–144.1 MHz) are reserved for CW only to preserve traditional weak-signal CW operation.

questions.question: How are US amateurs restricted in segments of bands where the Amateur Radio Service is secondary?
answers: U.S. amateurs may find non-amateur stations in those segments, and must avoid interfering with them
U.S. amateurs must give foreign amateur stations priority in those segments
International communications are not permitted in those segments
Digital transmissions are not permitted in those segments
questions.explanation: When the Amateur Radio Service is secondary, primary service users have priority. Amateurs must not cause interference to primary users and must accept any interference from them.

questions.question: Why should you not set your transmit frequency to be exactly at the edge of an amateur band or sub-band?
answers: To allow for calibration error in the transmitter frequency display
So that modulation sidebands do not extend beyond the band edge
To allow for transmitter frequency drift
questions.explanation: Staying away from band edges accounts for display calibration errors, sidebands extending beyond the carrier, and frequency drift due to temperature changes. Any one of these could push your signal out-of-band.

questions.question: Where may SSB phone be used in amateur bands above 50 MHz?
answers: Only in sub-bands allocated to General class or higher licensees
In at least some segment of all these bands
On any band if the power is limited to 25 watts
questions.explanation: SSB phone operation is permitted in at least some segment of every amateur band above 50 MHz. Technician licensees can use SSB in the appropriate sub-bands.

questions.question: What is the maximum peak envelope power output for Technician class operators in their HF band segments?
questions.explanation: Technician licensees are permitted up to 200 watts PEP on their HF privileges. This covers the CW sub-bands on 80, 40, and 15 meters and the phone/CW segment on 10 meters.

questions.question: Except for some specific restrictions, what is the maximum peak envelope power output for Technician class operators using frequencies above 30 MHz?
questions.explanation: The maximum legal amateur station power in the US is 1500 watts PEP. Technician licensees operating above 30 MHz are subject to this same general limit, though specific bands or modes may impose lower limits.

questions.question: For which classes of amateur radio licenses does the FCC currently issue new licenses?
answers: Technician, Technician Plus, General, Amateur Extra
questions.explanation: The FCC currently issues only three license classes: Technician, General, and Amateur Extra. The Novice, Advanced, and Technician Plus classes were discontinued.

questions.question: Who may select a desired call sign under the vanity call sign rules?
answers: Only a licensed amateur with a General or Amateur Extra Class license
Only a licensed amateur with an Amateur Extra Class license
Only a licensed amateur who has been licensed continuously for more than 10 years
questions.explanation: Any licensed amateur operator — Technician, General, or Amateur Extra — may apply for a vanity call sign through the FCC's vanity call sign program, subject to availability and format rules.

questions.question: What types of international communications are FCC-licensed amateur radio stations permitted to make?
answers: Communications incidental to the purposes of the Amateur Radio Service and remarks of a personal character
Communications incidental to conducting business or remarks of a personal nature
Only communications incidental to contest exchanges; all other communications are prohibited
Any communications that would be permitted by an international broadcast station
questions.explanation: International amateur communications are permitted when incidental to the purposes of the Amateur Radio Service or of a personal character. Business communications are not permitted over amateur radio.

questions.question: What may happen if the FCC is unable to reach you by email?
answers: Fine and suspension of operator license
Revocation of the station license or suspension of the operator license
Revocation of access to the license record in the FCC system
Nothing; there is no such requirement
questions.explanation: FCC rules require licensees to maintain a valid email address in the ULS database. If the FCC cannot contact you and determines this is willful, your station license could be revoked or your operator license suspended.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid Group D call sign format for Technician class?
questions.explanation: New Technician licenses are typically issued in a 1×3 format (one letter prefix, one region digit, three suffix letters), such as KF1XXX. KA1X is a 1×1 format (Extra class) and W1XX is a 1×2 format.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about using your amateur radio license when operating aboard a vessel or craft in international waters?
answers: Amateur operation is prohibited in international waters
You may only operate during maritime emergencies
You need special FCC authorization for maritime mobile operation
You may operate from a US-documented vessel with the master's permission
questions.explanation: An FCC-licensed amateur may operate from a US-documented vessel in international waters with the master's permission. Operating from foreign countries requires compliance with that country's regulations.

questions.question: How long before the expiration date may an amateur radio license renewal be requested?
questions.explanation: You may renew your amateur radio license up to 90 days before it expires. Renewing early ensures continuous coverage and avoids operating during a lapsed period.

questions.question: What is the normal term for an FCC-issued amateur radio license?
questions.explanation: FCC amateur radio licenses are issued for a term of ten years. After ten years the license must be renewed; there is a two-year grace period after expiration during which you may renew but not transmit.

questions.question: What is the grace period for renewal if an amateur license expires?
questions.explanation: An expired amateur license has a two-year grace period during which you can still renew it. However, you may NOT transmit during this grace period until the renewal is processed and appears in the FCC database.

questions.question: How soon after passing the examination for your first amateur radio license may you transmit on the amateur radio bands?
answers: Immediately on receiving your Certificate of Successful Completion of Examination (CSCE)
As soon as your operator/station license grant appears on the ARRL website
As soon as your operator/station license grant appears in the FCC's license database
As soon as you receive your license in the mail from the FCC
questions.explanation: You may transmit only after your license grant appears in the FCC's Universal Licensing System (ULS) database. The CSCE proves you passed but is not a license. The FCC no longer mails paper licenses.

questions.question: If your license has expired and is still within the allowable grace period, may you continue to transmit on the amateur radio bands?
answers: Yes, for up to two years
Yes, as soon as you apply for renewal
Yes, for up to one year
No, you must wait until the license has been renewed
questions.explanation: During the two-year grace period after license expiration, you may NOT transmit. You must wait until the renewed license grant actually appears in the FCC ULS database before resuming amateur radio operation.

questions.question: With which countries are FCC-licensed amateur radio stations prohibited from exchanging communications?
answers: Any country whose administration has notified the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) that it objects to such communications
Any country whose administration has notified the American Radio Relay League (ARRL) that it objects to such communications
Any country banned from such communications by the International Amateur Radio Union (IARU)
Any country banned from making such communications by the American Radio Relay League (ARRL)
questions.explanation: FCC rules prohibit amateur communications with any country whose government has officially notified the ITU that it objects to such contacts. This is governed through the ITU framework, not private organizations like ARRL or IARU.

questions.question: Under which of the following circumstances are one-way transmissions by an amateur station prohibited?
answers: Announcements of upcoming ham radio operating events
questions.explanation: Broadcasting — transmitting one-way communications intended for reception by the general public — is prohibited. One-way transmissions are permitted for beacons, telecommand, telemetry, code practice, and emergency bulletins.

questions.question: When is it permissible to transmit messages encoded to obscure their meaning?
answers: Only when using a remote station during a contest
Only when transmitting certain approved digital codes
Only when transmitting control commands to space stations or model craft
questions.explanation: Amateur communications must be in plain language. The only exception allowing encoded transmissions is when sending control commands to space stations or radio-controlled model craft.

questions.question: Under what conditions is an amateur station authorized to transmit music using a phone emission?
answers: When incidental to an authorized retransmission of manned spacecraft communications
When the music produces no spurious emissions
When transmissions are limited to less than three minutes per hour
When the music is transmitted above 1280 MHz
questions.explanation: Music is generally prohibited on amateur radio, but an exception exists when it is incidental to an authorized retransmission of manned spacecraft communications (such as relaying NASA audio that happens to include music).

questions.question: When may amateur radio operators use their stations to notify other amateurs of the availability of equipment for sale or trade?
answers: When the equipment is not the personal property of either the station licensee, or the control operator, or their close relatives
When no profit is made on the sale
When selling amateur radio equipment and not on a regular basis
questions.explanation: Amateurs may announce personal amateur radio equipment for sale or trade, but only when it is their own equipment and not done on a regular basis (which would constitute commercial activity).

questions.question: What, if any, are the restrictions concerning transmission of language that may be considered indecent or obscene?
answers: The FCC maintains a list of words that are not permitted to be used on amateur frequencies
The International Telecommunications Union (ITU) maintains a list of words that are not permitted to be used on amateur frequencies
questions.explanation: FCC rules prohibit any obscene or indecent language on amateur radio. There is no specific word list; any language considered obscene or indecent is prohibited under Part 97.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an auxiliary station?
answers: A station sending one-way transmissions between a remote repeater receiver and the main repeater transmitter
A backup radio for emergency use in case the main station radio fails
A station used in the Military Auxiliary Radio System for linking government and amateur stations in a digital network
A second station utilized in multi-operator contest stations
questions.explanation: An auxiliary station sends one-way transmissions, such as linking a remote repeater receiver to the main repeater transmitter. This is a common use case in repeater systems.

questions.question: In which of the following circumstances may the control operator of an amateur station receive compensation for operating that station?
answers: When the communication is related to the sale of amateur equipment by the control operator's employer
When the communication is a part of classroom instruction at an educational institution
When the communication is made to obtain emergency information for a local broadcast station
questions.explanation: An amateur may receive compensation for operating a station when the communication is incidental to classroom instruction at an educational institution. This is the primary exception to the general rule against compensated operation.

questions.question: When may amateur stations transmit information in support of broadcasting, program production, or news gathering, assuming no other means is available?
answers: When such communications are directly related to the immediate safety of human life or protection of property
When broadcasting communications to or from the space shuttle
Where non-commercial programming is gathered and supplied exclusively to the National Public Radio network
questions.explanation: Amateur stations may support broadcasting or news gathering only when communications are directly related to the immediate safety of human life or protection of property and no other means is available.

questions.question: How does the FCC define broadcasting for the Amateur Radio Service?
answers: Any transmission made by the licensed station
Transmission of messages directed only to amateur operators
Transmissions intended for reception by the general public
questions.explanation: In Part 97, broadcasting means transmissions intended for reception by the general public. Amateur radio is a two-way communication service; one-way transmissions intended for anyone to receive are prohibited.

questions.question: When may an amateur station transmit without identifying on the air?
answers: When the transmissions are of a brief nature to make station adjustments
When the transmitted power level is below 0.1 watt
When transmitting signals to control model craft
questions.explanation: The one situation where an amateur station may transmit without identifying is when transmitting signals to control model craft (radio-controlled aircraft, boats, etc.). All other transmissions require identification.

questions.question: Which of the following is required when making on-the-air test transmissions?
answers: Conduct tests only between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. local time
Notify the FCC of the transmissions
questions.explanation: All amateur transmissions, including test transmissions, must include proper station identification. There are no time restrictions on testing, and FCC notification is not required.

questions.question: When may an amateur station transmit without a control operator?
answers: When using automatic control, such as in the case of a repeater
When the station licensee is away and another licensed amateur is using the station
When the transmitting station is an auxiliary station
questions.explanation: FCC rules require a control operator for all amateur transmissions at all times. Even automatically controlled stations (like repeaters) must have a designated control operator, though that person need not be at the station.

questions.question: Who may be the control operator of a station communicating through an amateur satellite or space station?
answers: Only an Amateur Extra Class operator
A General class or higher licensee with a satellite operator certification
Only an Amateur Extra Class operator who is also an AMSAT member
Any amateur allowed to transmit on the satellite uplink frequency
questions.explanation: Any licensed amateur with privileges on the satellite uplink frequency may be the control operator for satellite communications. No special certification beyond your license is required.

questions.question: Who must designate the station control operator?
questions.explanation: The station licensee is responsible for designating the control operator. The licensee may operate the station themselves or designate another licensed amateur as control operator.

questions.question: What determines the transmitting frequency privileges of an amateur station?
answers: The frequency authorized by the frequency coordinator
The frequencies printed on the license grant
The highest class of operator license held by anyone on the premises
The class of operator license held by the control operator
questions.explanation: The control operator's license class determines what frequencies the station may use. A station with an Extra class licensee present can only operate in Extra sub-bands if the Extra licensee is the designated control operator.

questions.question: What is an amateur station's control point?
answers: The location of the station's transmitting antenna
The location of the station's transmitting apparatus
The location at which the control operator function is performed
The mailing address of the station licensee
questions.explanation: The control point is the location where the control operator function is performed — where the operator monitors and controls the station. For a remotely controlled station, this is where the operator sits, not where the transmitter is located.

questions.question: When, other than during an emergency, may a Technician class licensee be the control operator of a station operating in an Amateur Extra Class band segment?
answers: When designated as the control operator by an Amateur Extra Class licensee
As part of a multi-operator contest team
When using a club station whose trustee holds an Amateur Extra Class license
questions.explanation: A Technician class licensee may never be the control operator for a station transmitting in an Amateur Extra Class exclusive sub-band (outside of an emergency). Operating privileges are limited by the control operator's own license class.

questions.question: When the control operator is not the station licensee, who is responsible for the proper operation of the station?
answers: All licensed amateurs who are present at the operation
The control operator and the station licensee
questions.explanation: Both the control operator and the station licensee share responsibility for proper operation. The control operator is directly responsible for transmissions, while the station licensee is ultimately responsible for their station.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of automatic control?
answers: Controlling a station over the internet
Using a computer or other device to send CW automatically
Using a computer or other device to identify automatically
questions.explanation: Automatic control means the station operates without a control operator present — repeaters are the classic example. Internet-controlled stations are remote control, not automatic control.

questions.question: Which amateur stations may be remotely controlled?
questions.explanation: FCC rules permit any amateur station to be remotely controlled, provided a licensed control operator is monitoring and can control the station. There is no restriction to specific station types.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of remote control as defined in Part 97?
answers: Operating the station over the internet
Controlling a model aircraft, boat, or car by amateur radio
questions.explanation: Remote control means the control operator is at a control point separated from the transmitter. Operating a station over the internet is a typical example of remote control.

questions.question: What is a control operator as defined in Part 97?
answers: The person speaking or otherwise communicating messages over an amateur station
The person who is the licensee of an amateur station
An amateur operator identified in the FCC database as responsible for transmissions and FCC rules compliance at a station license location
An amateur operator designated by the licensee of a station to be responsible for transmissions and FCC rules compliance at that station
questions.explanation: The control operator is the licensed amateur designated by the station licensee to be responsible for the station's transmissions and FCC rules compliance. The control operator need not be the licensee.

questions.question: When must the station licensee make the station and the station records available for inspection?
answers: At any time ten days after notification by the FCC of such an inspection
At any time upon request by an FCC representative
At any time after a written notification by the FCC of such inspection
Only when presented with a valid warrant by an FCC official or government agent
questions.explanation: An amateur station and its records must be made available for inspection at any time upon request by an FCC representative. No advance notice or written notification is required.

questions.question: How often must you identify with your FCC-assigned call sign when using tactical call signs such as "Race Headquarters"?
answers: Never, the tactical call is sufficient
At least every 10 minutes during and at the end of a communication
At the end of every transmission
questions.explanation: Even when using tactical call signs for convenience during events, you must still identify with your FCC-assigned call sign at least every 10 minutes during and at the end of a communication.

questions.question: When are you required to transmit your assigned call sign?
answers: At the beginning of each contact, and every 10 minutes thereafter
At least once during each transmission
At least every 15 minutes during and at the end of a communication
At least every 10 minutes during and at the end of a communication
questions.explanation: FCC rules require station identification at least every 10 minutes during a communication and at the end of the communication. Identification at the beginning is good practice but not explicitly required.

questions.question: What language must you use for identification when using a phone emission?
answers: Any language recognized by the United Nations
Any language recognized by the ITU
questions.explanation: When identifying by phone (voice), you must use English for the call sign identification. Other languages may be used for the content of communications, but the ID itself must be in English.

questions.question: What method of call sign identification is required for a station transmitting phone signals?
answers: Send the call sign followed by the indicator RPT
Send the call sign using a CW or phone emission
Send the call sign followed by the indicator R
Send the call sign using only a phone emission
questions.explanation: For phone stations, identification may be given using either a CW or phone emission. You are not required to use voice — sending your call sign in Morse code while on a phone transmission is acceptable.

questions.question: Which of the following self-assigned indicators are acceptable when using a phone transmission?
questions.explanation: When operating with a self-assigned indicator (such as a portable or mobile designator), you may use any of the spoken terms — stroke, slant, or slash — to indicate the separator between your call sign and the indicator.

questions.question: Which of the following restrictions apply when a non-licensed person speaks to a foreign amateur radio station via a station under the control of an FCC-licensed amateur radio operator?
answers: The person must be a U.S. citizen
The foreign station must be in a country with which the U.S. has a third-party agreement
The licensed control operator must do the station identification
questions.explanation: Third-party communications with foreign stations are only permitted to countries that have a third-party agreement with the United States. There is no citizenship requirement for the third party.

questions.question: What is the definition of third-party communications?
answers: A message from a control operator to another amateur station control operator on behalf of another person
Amateur radio communications where three stations are in communications with one another
Operation when the transmitting equipment is licensed to a person other than the control operator
Temporary authorization for an unlicensed person to transmit on the amateur bands for technical experiments
questions.explanation: Third-party communications are messages passed between control operators on behalf of a third party (someone other than the licensed operators). The third party does not transmit.

questions.question: What type of amateur station simultaneously retransmits the signal of another amateur station on a different channel or channels?
questions.explanation: A repeater station receives a signal on one frequency and simultaneously retransmits it on a different frequency, extending the range of communications for mobile and portable stations.

questions.question: Who is accountable if a repeater inadvertently retransmits communications that violate the FCC rules?
answers: The control operator of the originating station
The control operator of the repeater
Both the originating station and the repeater owner
questions.explanation: The control operator of the originating station is accountable for the content of their transmissions, even when those transmissions are retransmitted by a repeater. The repeater owner is generally not held responsible for inadvertent retransmissions.

questions.question: Which of the following is a requirement for the issuance of a club station license grant?
answers: The trustee must have an Amateur Extra Class operator license grant
The club must have at least four members
The club must be registered with the American Radio Relay League (ARRL)
questions.explanation: FCC rules require that a club station have at least four members. The trustee must hold a Technician or higher license, but does not need to be Amateur Extra. ARRL registration is not required.

questions.question: What is a common repeater frequency offset in the 2-meter band?
questions.explanation: On the 2-meter band, repeaters typically use an offset of plus or minus 600 kHz between the transmit and receive frequencies. This is the standard offset used across most of the country.

questions.question: What is the national calling frequency for FM simplex operations in the 2-meter band?
questions.explanation: 146.520 MHz is the national FM simplex calling frequency for the 2-meter band. Operators call on this frequency to make initial contact, then move to another simplex frequency to continue the conversation.

questions.question: What is a common repeater frequency offset in the 70-centimeter band?
questions.explanation: On the 70-centimeter (440 MHz) band, repeaters typically use an offset of plus or minus 5 MHz. This larger offset accommodates the wider frequency range available on this band.

questions.question: What is an appropriate way to call another station on a repeater if you know the other station's call sign?
answers: Say "break, break," then the other station's call sign, followed by your call sign
Say the station's call sign, then identify with your call sign
Say "CQ" three times, then the other station's call sign, followed by your call sign
Wait for the station to call CQ, then answer with your call sign
questions.explanation: To call a specific station on a repeater, say the other station's call sign followed by your own call sign. "Break, break" is used for emergency interruptions, and "CQ" is used when calling for any station.

questions.question: How should you respond to a station calling CQ?
answers: Transmit "CQ" followed by the other station's call sign
Transmit your call sign followed by the other station's call sign
Transmit the other station's call sign followed by your call sign
Transmit a signal report followed by your call sign
questions.explanation: When responding to a CQ, transmit the calling station's call sign followed by your own call sign. This lets the CQ station know who is calling them specifically.

questions.question: What is an effective way to seek a call from any phone station when not using a repeater?
answers: Sign your call sign once, followed by the words "listening for a call;" if there is no answer, change the frequency and repeat
Say "QTC," followed by "this is" and your call sign; if there is no answer, change the frequency and repeat
Transmit an unmodulated carrier for approximately 10 seconds, followed by "this is" and your call sign, and pause to listen; repeat as necessary
Repeat "CQ" a few times, followed by "this is," and your call sign, then pause to listen; repeat as necessary
questions.explanation: A CQ call is the standard way to call for any station. Repeat "CQ" a few times, follow with "this is" and your call sign, then pause to listen for a response. Repeat as needed.

questions.question: What does the term "repeater offset" mean?
answers: The difference between a repeater's transmit and receive frequencies
The repeater has a time delay to prevent interference
The approximately half-second delay to allow for the "squelch tail" to be removed
The fee charged by the repeater owner or club to provide for maintenance
questions.explanation: The repeater offset is the difference between the repeater's transmit and receive frequencies. The repeater listens on one frequency (input) and retransmits on another (output) to allow simultaneous communication.

questions.question: What is the meaning of the procedural signal "CQ"?
answers: A shortened form of the term "Contest QSO"
"Communication Quality," used to indicate transmitted audio clarity
Only the called station should transmit
questions.explanation: CQ is the traditional calling signal meaning "I am calling any station" or "calling all stations." It invites any station that hears the call to respond.

questions.question: Which of the following is a customary way to indicate a station is listening on a repeater and looking for a contact?
answers: "CQ CQ" followed by the repeater's call sign
The station's call sign followed by the word "listening"
The repeater's call sign followed by the station's call sign
questions.explanation: On a repeater, a common way to indicate you are available for a contact is to transmit your own call sign followed by the word "listening" or sometimes "monitoring."

questions.question: What is a band plan, beyond the privileges established by the FCC?
answers: A voluntary guideline for using different modes or activities within an amateur band
A list of available net frequencies
A plan devised by a club to indicate frequency band usage
questions.explanation: A band plan is a voluntary agreement among amateur operators that suggests how different portions of a band should be used (e.g., CW, SSB, FM, digital). It is not FCC law but helps minimize interference between different operating modes.

questions.question: What term describes an amateur station that is transmitting and receiving on the same frequency?
questions.explanation: Simplex operation means transmitting and receiving on the same frequency, taking turns. Full duplex means transmitting and receiving on different frequencies simultaneously (like a telephone or repeater).

questions.question: What is the purpose of the reverse function on a VHF/UHF transceiver?
answers: To listen on a repeater's input frequency
To listen on a repeater's output frequency
questions.explanation: The reverse function swaps the transmit and receive frequencies, allowing you to listen on the repeater's input frequency. This is useful to check if a station is within direct range without the repeater.

questions.question: What term describes the use of a sub-audible tone transmitted along with normal voice audio to open the squelch of a receiver?
questions.explanation: CTCSS (Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System) uses a continuous sub-audible tone (below 300 Hz) transmitted with the audio to open a repeater or receiver configured to require that specific tone.

questions.question: Which of the following describes a linked repeater network?
answers: A network of repeaters in which signals received by one repeater are transmitted by all the repeaters in the network
A single repeater with more than one receiver
Multiple repeaters with the same control operator
A system of repeaters linked by APRS
questions.explanation: A linked repeater network connects multiple repeaters so that a signal received by one is simultaneously retransmitted by all of them. This greatly extends the coverage area.

questions.question: Which of the following could be the reason you are unable to access a repeater whose output you can hear?
answers: You are using the wrong CTCSS tone
You are using the wrong DCS code
questions.explanation: All three can prevent access: wrong offset means your transmission doesn't reach the repeater's input; wrong CTCSS or DCS code means the repeater won't open even if your signal arrives.

questions.question: Which of the following would cause your FM transmission audio to drop out on voice peaks?
answers: Your FM deviation is too low
Your transmit power is too high
questions.explanation: Talking too loudly causes excessive FM deviation (over-deviation), which can exceed the receiver's ability to demodulate the signal properly, causing audio to clip or drop out on loud voice peaks.

questions.question: What type of signaling to a repeater uses two simultaneous audio tones?
questions.explanation: DTMF (Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency) uses two simultaneous audio tones for each digit or character, the same technology used for telephone touch-tone dialing. It's used to send commands to repeaters and autopatch systems.

questions.question: How can you join a digital repeater's "talkgroup"?
answers: Register with the local Frequency Coordinator
Register with the digital repeater control operator
Program your radio with the group's ID or code
Program your radio with the DTMF tone used by the talkgroup
questions.explanation: To access a talkgroup on a digital (DMR) repeater, you program your radio with the talkgroup's numerical ID. No registration with any organization is required.

questions.question: Which of the following applies when two stations transmitting on the same frequency interfere with each other?
answers: The stations should negotiate continued use of the frequency
Both stations should choose another frequency to avoid conflict
Whichever station was on the frequency first has preemptive rights to the frequency
Use subaudible tones so both stations can share the frequency
questions.explanation: When two stations interfere with each other, the proper procedure is to negotiate — discuss the situation and decide together how to resolve it. No amateur has preemptive rights to a frequency.

questions.question: Why are simplex channels designated in the VHF/UHF band plans?
answers: So stations within range of each other can communicate without tying up a repeater
So stations with simple transmitters can access the repeater without automated offset
questions.explanation: Simplex channels allow stations that are close enough to communicate directly without using a repeater. This frees up the repeater for stations that actually need the extended range.

questions.question: Which Q signal indicates that you are receiving interference from other stations?
questions.explanation: QRM indicates interference from other stations. QRN indicates static or natural interference, QTH is your location, and QSB indicates signal fading.

questions.question: Which Q signal indicates that you are changing frequency?
questions.explanation: QSY means you are changing to another frequency. QSL means acknowledgment/receipt, QRZ means "who is calling me?", and QRU means you have nothing more to send.

questions.question: What is the digital color code used on DMR repeater systems?
answers: An access code which must be programmed into a DMR transmitter to access a specific repeater
A code which automatically programs the repeater offset to a frequency chosen by the user
A code which identifies the specific CODEC being used so that the repeater can properly decode the audio
A code transmitted by the repeater to indicate health and status of the equipment
questions.explanation: In DMR, the color code (0–15) functions like a CTCSS tone — it must match between the radio and the repeater for the radio to access the repeater. It helps prevent unintended access on co-channel repeaters.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a squelch function?
answers: Reduce a CW transmitter's key clicks
Mute the receiver audio when a signal is not present
Eliminate parasitic oscillations in an RF amplifier
questions.explanation: Squelch mutes the receiver's audio output when no signal above a set threshold is present, eliminating the constant background noise heard between transmissions.

questions.question: Which of the following is a "talkgroup"?
answers: A group of amateur radio operators who share email on a specific amateur radio topic
An identifier used by DMR to organize radio traffic so that those who want to hear the group aren't bothered by other radio traffic
The members of a net organized for amateur radio operators with a specific common interest
A method of automatically alerting all group members to the frequency where any member is transmitting
questions.explanation: A talkgroup is a DMR digital radio concept — a numerical identifier that organizes radio traffic. Radios programmed with a specific talkgroup ID will only hear traffic on that group, filtering out other activity on the same repeater.

questions.question: When do the FCC Part 97 Amateur Radio Service rules NOT apply to the operation of an amateur station?
questions.explanation: FCC Part 97 rules always apply to the operation of amateur stations. RACES, ARES, and FEMA involvement does not suspend FCC regulations. Operators must always follow Part 97.

questions.question: Which of the following are typical duties of a Net Control Station?
answers: Choose the regular net meeting time and frequency
Ensure that all stations checking into the net are properly licensed for operation on the net frequency
Call the net to order and direct communications between stations checking in
questions.explanation: The Net Control Station (NCS) calls the net to order and manages traffic by directing communications. Verifying licenses and setting schedules are administrative tasks, not the NCS's real-time duties.

questions.question: What technique is used to ensure that voice messages containing unusual words are received correctly?
answers: Send the words by voice and Morse code
Use the Q-code "QSR" to ask the receiving station to repeat the words back
Spell the words using a standard phonetic alphabet
questions.explanation: The standard phonetic alphabet (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie...) is used to spell out unusual words, call signs, or any text that might be misunderstood due to poor signal conditions.

questions.question: What is RACES?
answers: An emergency organization combining amateur radio and citizens band operators and frequencies
A radio contest held in a short period, sometimes called a "sprint"
An FCC Part 97 amateur radio service for civil defense communications during national emergencies
questions.explanation: RACES (Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service) is an FCC Part 97 radio service established for civil defense communications during national emergencies. It requires operators to be enrolled in and certified by a civil defense organization.

questions.question: What does the term "traffic" refer to in net operation?
answers: Formal messages exchanged by net stations
The number of stations checking in and out of a net
Operation by mobile or portable stations
A count of the number of activations of the net each month
questions.explanation: In amateur radio net terminology, "traffic" refers to formal messages (radiograms) that are originated, relayed, and delivered through the net's message handling system.

questions.question: What is the Amateur Radio Emergency Service (ARES)?
answers: A group of licensed amateurs who have voluntarily registered their qualifications and equipment for communications duty in the public service
A group of licensed amateurs who are members of the military and who voluntarily agreed to provide message handling services in the case of an emergency
A training program that provides licensing courses for those interested in obtaining an amateur license to use during emergencies
A training program that certifies amateur operators for membership in the Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service
questions.explanation: ARES is an ARRL program of licensed amateurs who voluntarily register their qualifications and equipment for public service communications during emergencies. Unlike RACES, ARES operators do not need civil defense certification.

questions.question: Which of the following is standard practice when you participate in a net?
answers: When first responding to the net control station, transmit your call sign, name, and address as in the FCC database
Record the time of each of your transmissions
Unless you are reporting an emergency, transmit only when directed by the net control station
questions.explanation: Good net discipline requires transmitting only when directed by the Net Control Station, unless reporting an emergency. This keeps the net organized and prevents chaos.

questions.question: Which of the following relays messages using email addresses based on amateur callsigns?
questions.explanation: Winlink is an email-based system that uses amateur call signs as addresses (e.g., callsign@winlink.org). It allows amateurs to send and receive email messages via radio, useful during emergencies when the internet is unavailable.

questions.question: Are amateur station control operators ever permitted to operate outside the frequency privileges of their license class?
answers: Yes, but only when part of a FEMA emergency plan
Yes, but only when part of a RACES emergency plan
Yes, but only in situations involving the immediate safety of human life or protection of property
questions.explanation: In genuine emergencies involving immediate safety of human life or property protection, operators may use any frequency necessary. This is a narrow exception — it does not apply to FEMA or RACES drills, only actual immediate emergencies.

questions.question: What information is contained in the preamble of a formal traffic message?
answers: The email address of the originating station
The address of the intended recipient
The telephone number of the addressee
Information needed to track the message
questions.explanation: The preamble of a radiogram contains tracking information: message number, station of origin, precedence, handling instructions, originating station call sign, check (word count), place and date of origin. This allows the message to be tracked through the relay system.

questions.question: What is meant by "check" in a radiogram header?
answers: The number of words or word equivalents in the text portion of the message
The call sign of the originating station
A list of stations that have relayed the message
A box on the message form that indicates that the message was received and/or relayed
questions.explanation: The "check" is the word count of the text portion of the radiogram. It helps the receiving station verify that the entire message was received correctly and that no words were lost in transmission.

questions.question: Which of the following requires certification by a civil defense agency?
questions.explanation: RACES operators must be certified by and enrolled in a civil defense organization. ARES has no such requirement. MARS (Military Auxiliary Radio System) involves military certification, and SKYWARN is a weather-spotting program with no civil defense requirement.

questions.question: Why do VHF signal strengths sometimes vary greatly when the antenna is moved only a few feet?
answers: The signal path encounters different concentrations of water vapor
VHF ionospheric propagation is very sensitive to path length
Multipath propagation cancels or reinforces signals
The Doppler effect causes slight frequency shifts which result in changes in signal strength
questions.explanation: VHF signals can arrive via multiple paths (direct and reflected). When these signals are in phase they reinforce each other; when out of phase they cancel. Moving the antenna a short distance can change the phase relationship dramatically.

questions.question: How does vegetation affect UHF and microwave signals?
answers: Causes knife-edge diffraction, distorting voice peaks
Absorbs signals, leading to poor reception of weak signals
Amplifies signals, improving reception of weak signals
questions.explanation: Vegetation (trees, bushes) absorbs UHF and microwave signals, causing significant attenuation. Wet vegetation absorbs even more signal than dry. This is a significant path loss factor for these frequencies.

questions.question: What antenna polarization is normally used for long-distance CW and SSB contacts on the VHF and UHF bands?
questions.explanation: Horizontal polarization is the convention for weak-signal SSB and CW work on VHF and UHF. Using horizontal antennas on both ends prevents the 20 dB polarization loss that would occur with mismatched polarizations.

questions.question: What is the effect of antenna cross-polarization over a line-of-sight VHF or UHF path?
questions.explanation: When transmitting and receiving antennas have different polarizations (e.g., one vertical, one horizontal), the received signal strength is significantly reduced — typically by 20 dB or more.

questions.question: When using a directional antenna, how might your station be able to communicate with a distant repeater if buildings or obstructions are blocking the direct line of sight path?
answers: Change from vertical to horizontal polarization
Try to find a path that reflects signals to the repeater
questions.explanation: VHF/UHF signals can reflect off buildings, hills, and other surfaces. By pointing the directional antenna at a reflective surface rather than directly at the repeater, you may find a usable reflected path around an obstruction.

questions.question: What is the meaning of the term "picket fencing"?
answers: Alternating transmissions during a net operation
Rapid flutter on mobile signals due to multipath propagation
A type of ground system used with vertical antennas
Interference from cable TV in the form of carriers at fixed intervals across the band
questions.explanation: Picket fencing is the rapid, rhythmic flutter heard on mobile VHF/UHF signals caused by multipath interference as the vehicle moves through areas where signals arrive via multiple paths that alternately reinforce and cancel.

questions.question: What weather condition might decrease range at microwave frequencies?
questions.explanation: Rain, snow, and other precipitation absorb and scatter microwave signals, reducing their range. At frequencies above about 10 GHz, rainfall can cause significant attenuation.

questions.question: What is a likely cause of irregular fading of signals propagated by the ionosphere?
answers: Frequency shift due to Faraday rotation
Random combining of signals arriving via different paths
questions.explanation: Ionospheric signals often travel via multiple paths of slightly different lengths. These paths combine randomly at the receiver, sometimes adding and sometimes canceling, causing the characteristic irregular fading.

questions.question: Which of the following results from the fact that signals propagated by the ionosphere are elliptically polarized?
answers: Either vertically or horizontally polarized antennas may be used for transmission or reception
Both the transmitting and receiving antennas must be of the same polarization
questions.explanation: The ionosphere rotates the polarization of passing signals (Faraday rotation), resulting in elliptical polarization at the receiver. This means either vertical or horizontal antennas can receive the signal — polarization matching is not critical for HF.

questions.question: What effect does multi-path propagation have on data transmissions?
answers: Transmission rates must be increased by a factor equal to the number of separate paths observed
Transmission rates must be decreased by a factor equal to the number of separate paths observed
No significant changes will occur if the signals are transmitted using FM
Error rates are likely to increase
questions.explanation: Multipath propagation causes the same signal to arrive at slightly different times via different paths. These delayed copies can interfere with subsequent symbols, causing inter-symbol interference and increasing error rates in digital communications.

questions.question: Which region of the atmosphere can reflect HF radio waves?
questions.explanation: The ionosphere, a region of ionized gas approximately 60–1000 km above Earth, can refract (bend) HF radio waves back to Earth, enabling long-distance communications. The troposphere affects VHF/UHF through ducting.

questions.question: What effect does fog or rain have on 10-meter and 6-meter band signals?
questions.explanation: At 10 and 6 meters, fog and rain have little effect on signal propagation. Significant weather-related absorption only becomes a factor at microwave frequencies (above about 10 GHz).

questions.question: What is the relationship between the electric and magnetic fields of an electromagnetic wave?
questions.explanation: In an electromagnetic wave, the electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular (at right angles) to each other and to the direction of wave propagation. This orthogonal relationship is a fundamental property of EM waves.

questions.question: What property of a radio wave defines its polarization?
answers: The orientation of the electric field
The orientation of the magnetic field
The ratio of the energy in the magnetic field to the energy in the electric field
The ratio of the velocity to the wavelength
questions.explanation: Polarization is defined by the orientation of the electric field vector of the radio wave. If the electric field is vertical, the wave is vertically polarized; if horizontal, it is horizontally polarized.

questions.question: What are the two components of a radio wave?
questions.explanation: A radio wave consists of two components: an electric field and a magnetic field, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation. Together they form the electromagnetic wave.

questions.question: What is the velocity of a radio wave traveling through free space?
questions.explanation: Radio waves, like all electromagnetic radiation, travel at the speed of light (approximately 300,000,000 meters per second) in free space. They travel slightly slower in other media.

questions.question: What is the relationship between wavelength and frequency?
answers: Wavelength gets longer as frequency increases
Wavelength gets shorter as frequency increases
Wavelength is constant at all frequencies
Wavelength and frequency increase as path length increases
questions.explanation: Wavelength and frequency are inversely proportional: as frequency increases, wavelength decreases. This is expressed by the formula: wavelength = speed of light / frequency.

questions.question: What is the formula for converting frequency to approximate wavelength in meters?
answers: Wavelength in meters equals frequency in hertz multiplied by 300
Wavelength in meters equals frequency in hertz divided by 300
Wavelength in meters equals frequency in megahertz divided by 300
Wavelength in meters equals 300 divided by frequency in megahertz
questions.explanation: Wavelength (meters) = 300 / frequency (MHz). For example, the 2-meter band at 146 MHz: 300/146 ≈ 2.05 meters. This is derived from λ = c/f where c = 300,000,000 m/s.

questions.question: In addition to frequency, which of the following is used to identify amateur radio bands?
questions.explanation: Amateur bands are commonly referred to by their approximate wavelength in meters — the 2-meter band, the 70-centimeter band, the 10-meter band, etc. This is a long-standing tradition in amateur radio.

questions.question: What frequency range is referred to as VHF?
questions.explanation: VHF (Very High Frequency) spans 30 MHz to 300 MHz. This includes the popular 6-meter (50 MHz) and 2-meter (144 MHz) amateur bands.

questions.question: What frequency range is referred to as UHF?
questions.explanation: UHF (Ultra High Frequency) spans 300 MHz to 3000 MHz (3 GHz). This includes the 70-centimeter band (420–450 MHz) used for many FM repeaters.

questions.question: What frequency range is referred to as HF?
questions.explanation: HF (High Frequency) spans 3 to 30 MHz. This range includes the traditional shortwave bands used for long-distance communications via ionospheric propagation.

questions.question: What is the approximate velocity of a radio wave in free space?
questions.explanation: The speed of light (and radio waves) in free space is approximately 300,000,000 meters per second (3 × 10⁸ m/s). This is about 186,000 miles per second.

questions.question: Which of these frequencies travels at the highest velocity in free space?
answers: All radio frequencies travel at the same velocity
questions.explanation: All electromagnetic waves, regardless of frequency, travel at the same speed — the speed of light — in free space. Frequency determines wavelength, not velocity.

questions.question: Why are simplex UHF signals rarely heard beyond their radio horizon?
answers: They are too weak to go very far
FCC regulations prohibit them from going more than 50 miles
UHF signals are usually not propagated by the ionosphere
UHF signals are absorbed by the ionospheric D region
questions.explanation: UHF signals pass through the ionosphere rather than being reflected by it, so they are limited to line-of-sight distances. The ionosphere that provides long-distance HF propagation does not help UHF.

questions.question: What is a characteristic of HF communication compared with communications on VHF and higher frequencies?
answers: Long-distance ionospheric propagation is far more common on HF
There is less atmospheric interference (static) on HF
questions.explanation: HF signals (3–30 MHz) can be refracted by the ionosphere to enable worldwide communication, a capability rarely available on VHF and above. HF antennas are actually larger (longer wavelengths) and HF has more atmospheric static.

questions.question: What is one characteristic of VHF signals received via auroral backscatter?
answers: They are often received from 10,000 miles or more
They are distorted, with a characteristic raspy sound
They occur only during winter nighttime hours
They are generally strongest when your antenna is aimed west
questions.explanation: When VHF signals scatter off the aurora, the received signal has a characteristic rough, raspy, or "buzzsaw" distortion caused by the rapidly moving ionized curtain of the aurora.

questions.question: Which of the following types of propagation is most commonly associated with occasional strong signals on the 10-, 6-, and 2-meter bands from beyond the radio horizon?
questions.explanation: Sporadic E (Es) propagation occurs when dense patches of ionization form in the E layer of the ionosphere, reflecting VHF signals that would normally pass through. It can produce surprisingly strong signals over distances of 500–1500 miles.

questions.question: Which of the following effects may allow radio signals to travel beyond obstructions between the transmitting and receiving stations?
questions.explanation: Knife-edge diffraction occurs when radio waves bend around the sharp edge of an obstruction (like a mountain ridge or building), allowing some signal to reach beyond the geometric shadow of the obstruction.

questions.question: What type of propagation is responsible for allowing over-the-horizon VHF and UHF communications to ranges of approximately 300 miles on a regular basis?
questions.explanation: Tropospheric ducting occurs when temperature inversions create a layer of higher-density air that acts as a waveguide, trapping VHF/UHF signals and allowing them to travel hundreds of miles beyond the normal radio horizon.

questions.question: What band is best suited for communicating via meteor scatter?
questions.explanation: The 6-meter band (50 MHz) is particularly well-suited for meteor scatter propagation. The ionized trails left by meteors burning up in the atmosphere reflect 6-meter signals over distances of 500–1200 miles.

questions.question: What causes tropospheric ducting?
answers: Discharges of lightning during electrical storms
questions.explanation: Tropospheric ducting is caused by temperature inversions — where a layer of warm air sits above cooler air near the surface. This creates a refractive layer that traps and guides VHF/UHF signals over long distances.

questions.question: What is generally the best time for long-distance 10-meter band propagation via the F region?
answers: From dawn to shortly after sunset during periods of high sunspot activity
From shortly after sunset to dawn during periods of high sunspot activity
From dawn to shortly after sunset during periods of low sunspot activity
From shortly after sunset to dawn during periods of low sunspot activity
questions.explanation: The F region ionization is maintained by solar radiation, so it is most effective during daylight hours. High sunspot activity increases ionization, enabling long-distance 10-meter propagation from dawn to shortly after sunset.

questions.question: Which of the following bands may provide long-distance communications via the ionosphere's F region during the peak of the sunspot cycle?
questions.explanation: During solar cycle peaks, the ionosphere's F layer can reflect signals up to about 50 MHz. This means both 10 meters (28 MHz) and 6 meters (50 MHz) can support worldwide propagation. UHF frequencies pass through the ionosphere.

questions.question: Why is the radio horizon for VHF and UHF signals more distant than the visual horizon?
answers: Radio signals move somewhat faster than the speed of light
Radio waves are not blocked by dust particles
The atmosphere refracts radio waves slightly
Radio waves are blocked by dust particles
questions.explanation: The atmosphere's density gradient slightly refracts (bends) radio waves downward, causing them to follow Earth's curvature a bit further than a straight line of sight. This extends the radio horizon about 15% beyond the geometric horizon.

questions.question: Which of the following is an appropriate power supply rating for a typical 50-watt output mobile FM transceiver?
questions.explanation: A 50-watt FM transceiver requires approximately 12–15 amperes at 13.8 volts (the standard automotive voltage). P = I×V, so 50W / 13.8V ≈ 3.6A receive, but transmit draw is much higher — about 10–12 amperes at 50 watts output.

questions.question: Which of the following should be considered when selecting an accessory SWR meter?
answers: The frequency and power level at which the measurements will be made
The distance that the meter will be located from the antenna
The maximum SWR anticipated on the transmission line
The ability of the meter to compensate for a poor transmission line match to the antenna
questions.explanation: SWR meters are rated for specific frequency ranges and power levels. A meter designed for HF won't work accurately at VHF, and a meter rated for 150W might be damaged or inaccurate at 1500W.

questions.question: Why are short, heavy-gauge wires used for a transceiver's DC power connection?
answers: To minimize voltage drop when transmitting
To provide a close match to the power supply output impedance
To minimize radiative losses in the power cable
questions.explanation: During transmit, the transceiver draws high current. Long or thin wires have significant resistance, causing voltage drop under load. Short, heavy gauge wire keeps the voltage drop minimal to maintain full power output.

questions.question: How are the audio input and output of a transceiver connected in a station configured to operate using FT8?
answers: To a computer running a terminal program and connected to a terminal node controller unit
To the audio output and input of a computer running FT8 software
To an FT8 conversion unit, a keyboard, and a computer monitor
To a computer connected to the FT8converter.com website
questions.explanation: FT8 is a computer-generated digital mode. The transceiver's audio output (speaker) connects to the computer's audio input (microphone), and the computer's audio output (speaker) connects to the transceiver's audio input (microphone). FT8 software generates and decodes the audio tones.

questions.question: Where should an RF power meter be installed?
answers: In the feed line, between the transmitter and antenna
In parallel with the push-to-talk line and the antenna
In the power supply cable, as close as possible to the radio
questions.explanation: An RF power meter must be installed in the RF feed line between the transmitter and antenna to measure the actual RF power being delivered to the antenna system.

questions.question: What signals are used in a computer-radio interface for digital mode operation?
answers: Receive and transmit mode, status, and location
Receive audio, transmit audio, and transmitter keying
NMEA GPS location and DC power
questions.explanation: A computer-radio interface for digital modes needs three connections: receive audio (from radio to computer), transmit audio (from computer to radio), and a transmitter keying line (PTT) to switch the radio from receive to transmit.

questions.question: Which of the following is one of the connections required between a computer and a transceiver to operate digital modes?
answers: Computer "line in" to transceiver speaker connector
Computer "line out" to transceiver speaker connector
questions.explanation: To receive digital mode audio, the transceiver's speaker output connects to the computer's line-in (audio input). The computer then processes the received audio tones. The computer's line-out goes to the transceiver's microphone input for transmit.

questions.question: Which of the following conductors is preferred for bonding at RF?
answers: Copper braid removed from coaxial cable
questions.explanation: Flat copper strap has lower inductance than round wire at RF frequencies due to its large surface area. Inductance increases impedance at RF, so low-inductance connections are essential for effective RF bonding.

questions.question: How can you determine the length of time that equipment can be powered from a battery?
answers: Divide the watt-hour rating of the battery by the peak power consumption of the equipment
Divide the battery ampere-hour rating by the average current draw of the equipment
Multiply the watts per hour consumed by the equipment by the battery power rating
Multiply the square of the current rating of the battery by the input resistance of the equipment
questions.explanation: Battery capacity in ampere-hours (Ah) divided by average current draw (A) gives runtime in hours. For example, a 10 Ah battery powering a radio drawing an average of 2A would run for 5 hours.

questions.question: What function does a digital mode hotspot perform for nearby transceivers?
answers: Communication with a digital voice or data network
FT8 digital communications via AFSK using a smartphone connected to the internet
RTTY encoding and decoding without a computer
High-speed digital communications for meteor scatter
questions.explanation: A digital hotspot (such as for D-STAR, DMR, or System Fusion) is a personal gateway that allows a nearby radio to connect to digital voice or data networks via the internet, even without a nearby repeater.

questions.question: Where should the negative power return of a mobile transceiver be connected in a vehicle?
answers: To the shell of the power connector
To any metal part of the vehicle
questions.explanation: The negative power lead should connect directly to the vehicle's battery chassis ground to minimize ground loop interference and ensure the lowest possible resistance in the power circuit.

questions.question: What is an electronic keyer?
answers: A device for switching antennas from transmit to receive
A device for voice activated switching from receive to transmit
A device that assists in manual sending of Morse code
An interlock to prevent unauthorized use of a radio
questions.explanation: An electronic keyer assists in sending Morse code by automatically generating dots, dashes, and the proper spacing between them when you press the paddle contacts. It makes sending CW easier and more consistent.

questions.question: What is the effect of excessive microphone gain on SSB transmissions?
questions.explanation: Excessive microphone gain causes the audio to overdrive the transmitter's modulator, resulting in distorted, splashy audio that is difficult to understand and occupies excess bandwidth, causing interference to adjacent frequencies.

questions.question: Which of the following can be used to enter a transceiver's operating frequency?
questions.explanation: Transceivers allow frequency entry via a keypad (direct frequency entry) or a VFO (Variable Frequency Oscillator) tuning knob. CTCSS/DTMF and AFC serve other purposes.

questions.question: How is squelch adjusted so that a weak FM signal can be heard?
answers: Set the squelch threshold so that receiver output audio is on all the time
Turn up the audio level until it overcomes the squelch threshold
questions.explanation: To hear a weak signal, open the squelch completely by setting the threshold so the receiver outputs audio continuously (even with background noise). This allows the weak signal to be heard at the expense of also hearing noise when no signal is present.

questions.question: What does an FM signal sound like when received slightly off frequency?
answers: There is no effect except for reduction in amplitude
questions.explanation: FM reception is sensitive to being exactly on frequency. A slight offset causes audio distortion because the discriminator or ratio detector isn't processing the signal correctly. This is why FM receivers use automatic frequency control (AFC).

questions.question: What does the scanning function of an FM transceiver do?
answers: Tunes through a range of frequencies to check for activity
Tunes through a range of frequencies to determine the antenna's resonant frequency
questions.explanation: The scan function automatically cycles through programmed frequencies or a frequency range, pausing when it detects a signal above the squelch threshold. This lets you monitor multiple frequencies for activity.

questions.question: Which of the following controls could be used if the voice pitch of a single-sideband signal returning to your CQ call seems too high or low?
questions.explanation: The RIT (Receiver Incremental Tuning) or Clarifier adjusts the receive frequency independently of the transmit frequency, allowing you to fine-tune the received audio pitch on SSB without changing your transmit frequency.

questions.question: What is a DMR "code plug"?
answers: An adapter cable used to connect a DMR radio to a computer for internet access
Configuration data loaded onto your radio to access repeaters and talkgroups
An upgrade to DMR programming software provided by the radio manufacturer to accommodate new radio models
A Coder-Decoder (CODEC) that converts analog voice data to DMR digital data and vice versa
questions.explanation: A DMR code plug is a configuration file loaded into the radio that contains all the programmed channels, talkgroups, color codes, and other settings needed to use specific DMR repeater systems.

questions.question: What is the advantage of having a choice of receiver filter bandwidths in a multimode transceiver?
answers: Permits monitoring several modes simultaneously by selecting a separate filter for each mode
Permits noise or interference reduction by selecting a bandwidth matching the mode
Increases the number of frequencies that can be stored in memory
Increases the amount of offset between receive and transmit frequencies
questions.explanation: Using a filter bandwidth that matches the signal bandwidth passes the signal while rejecting noise and interference outside the signal's bandwidth. A CW signal needs only 500 Hz; using a 3 kHz filter admits unnecessary noise.

questions.question: How is a specific group of stations selected on a DMR digital voice transceiver?
answers: By retrieving the frequencies from transceiver memory
By enabling the group's CTCSS tone
By entering the group's identification code
By inserting a five-pin, pre-programmed code plug
questions.explanation: On DMR, you select a specific talkgroup by entering or programming the group's numerical identification code. This can be programmed in the code plug or entered manually on some radios.

questions.question: Which of the following receiver filter bandwidths provides the best signal-to-noise ratio for SSB reception?
questions.explanation: SSB voice signals occupy approximately 2.4–3 kHz of bandwidth. A 2400 Hz filter passes the voice signal while rejecting noise outside that range. A 500 Hz filter would cut important voice frequencies; a 5000 Hz filter admits unnecessary noise.

questions.question: Which of the following must be programmed into a D-STAR digital transceiver before transmitting?
questions.explanation: D-STAR transmitters must have the operator's call sign programmed before transmitting. The call sign is embedded in the digital transmission and is used for identification and routing through the D-STAR network.

questions.question: Electrical current is measured in which of the following units?
questions.explanation: Current (the flow of electrons) is measured in amperes (amps, A). Volts measure electrical potential (voltage), watts measure power, and ohms measure resistance.

questions.question: Electrical power is measured in which of the following units?
questions.explanation: Power is measured in watts (W). Watt-hours (Wh) measure energy (power over time), volts measure potential difference, and amperes measure current flow.

questions.question: What is the term for the flow of electrons in an electric circuit?
questions.explanation: Current is the term for the flow of electrons in a circuit, measured in amperes. Voltage is the electrical force that drives current; resistance opposes its flow.

questions.question: What term describes the number of times per second that an alternating current makes a complete cycle?
questions.explanation: Frequency describes how many complete cycles per second an AC signal completes, measured in hertz (Hz). One hertz equals one cycle per second.

questions.question: A difference in which of the following causes electron flow?
questions.explanation: Voltage (electromotive force, EMF) is the electrical pressure or potential difference that drives electrons through a circuit. It is measured in volts (V).

questions.question: What is the unit of frequency?
questions.explanation: Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), which equals one cycle per second. Henry is the unit of inductance, and farad is the unit of capacitance.

questions.question: Why are metals generally good conductors of electricity?
answers: They have relatively high Young's modulus values
questions.explanation: Metals have a "sea" of free electrons in their atomic structure that can move easily from atom to atom when a voltage is applied. This free movement of electrons is what makes metals good conductors.

questions.question: Which of the following is a good electrical insulator?
questions.explanation: Glass has very few free electrons and high electrical resistance, making it an excellent insulator. Sea water is a conductor (dissolved salts), stainless steel and graphite are conductors.

questions.question: Which of the following describes alternating current?
answers: Current that alternates between a positive direction and zero
Current that alternates between a negative direction and zero
Current that alternates between positive and negative directions
